- [TEMPORAL] Session Date: 2023/05/21 (Sun) 15:43
- [USER] User inquired about converting the steering wheel angle of a car to the actual wheel angle.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The steering wheel angle of a car is converted to the actual wheel angle through Ackermann steering geometry, which uses the principle of parallel steering.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The inner wheel on a turn must rotate through a smaller angle than the outer wheel.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The specific calculations for the conversion depend on the make and model of the car and the steering system used.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The steering ratio, which is the ratio of steering wheel rotation to wheel rotation, is usually provided in the car's specifications and can be used for conversion.
- [USER] User asked for clarification on the term "track width."
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Track width is the distance between the center of the left wheel and the center of the right wheel on the same axle of a vehicle.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Track width is typically measured on the front wheels and affects the handling and stability of a car.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] A wider track width can provide better stability, while a narrower track width can make a car more agile.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Track width is also referred to as wheelbase, which is the distance between the center of the front wheel and the center of the rear wheel.
- [USER] User inquired about the definition of "turning circle."
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The turning circle, or turning radius, is the diameter of the smallest circle that a vehicle can turn around within.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] It is measured from the center of the front wheel to the point where the front wheel contacts the ground during a full U-turn.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] The turning circle is important for determining a vehicle's maneuverability in tight spaces.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] It is calculated by turning the steering wheel to the maximum lock and measuring the distance as described.
- [USER] User asked if most private cars use Ackermann steering geometry.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Most private cars use Ackermann steering geometry, which employs the principle of parallel steering.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] In Ackermann steering, the inner wheel rotates through a smaller angle than the outer wheel.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Ackermann geometry is widely used in various vehicles, including passenger cars, trucks, buses, and some heavy equipment.
- [ASSISTANT_SAID] Some high-performance and race cars use different steering geometries like "four-wheel steering" or "active steering."
